I'm 78 years old this year, and I've farmed these fields for 55 years. I finished middle school, so I can read and figure out what the extension technician is talking about when he explains fertilizer rates, but honestly, what I learned from my father and what I've seen with my own eyes matters more than anything on paper.

I only have 4.1 mu, which is small even for our village. About 3 mu I keep in wheat-maize rotation — that's my bread and butter. The remaining 1.1 mu I plant cotton for cash, though I grow less of it now because at my age the picking is hard on my back, and it's just me and my wife managing everything.

For the wheat, I plant in mid-October with a local improved variety I've been using for years. The extension guy recommends about 15 kg of nitrogen per mu, and I aim for roughly that — I apply half as compound fertilizer at planting, and half as urea at jointing in the spring. I irrigate three times if I can afford the pumping: winter irrigation if it's dry, once at green-up, and once at heading. My neighbor Zhang only does two, but I've had years where that third irrigation made the difference between 350 and 420 kg per mu.

The maize goes in the same 3 mu right after wheat harvest, usually around June 12th. The turnaround is brutal — sometimes only 4 or 5 days — so I hire a combine harvester for the wheat. It costs money, but at my age I can't cut 3 mu by hand, and I need the time to plant the maize. I use hybrid seed, which is more expensive, but the yield gain pays for itself. I put down about 14 kg of nitrogen per mu as compound fertilizer at planting, all at once. I irrigate twice: at jointing and filling. I don't usually topdress maize because by then I'm busy with cotton and my wife and I can only do so much.

Cotton is on the 1.1 mu. I plant in late April. I apply around 11 kg of nitrogen per mu — base at planting, then another dose at flowering. Cotton pests are relentless here, so I spray insecticide three or four times and herbicide once. I irrigate twice, at flowering and boll stage. The real problem is picking. My wife and I do what we can, but I have to hire about five days of labor in September and October. At 120 yuan per day, that's 600 yuan gone, but I physically can't bend that long anymore.

I expect about 420 kg/mu from wheat, 450 kg/mu from maize, and 230 kg/mu of lint from cotton. I'm not trying to win any yield contests — I just need enough to cover our costs, pay for medicine, and have a little left over. At 78, stability is worth more than gambling on some new variety or technique.
